summary.one_liner: A curated reading list of articles, talks and engineering blog posts describing how large-scale systems at companies like Google, Netflix, Uber and LinkedIn handle scalability, availability, stability, performance, data and architecture.
summary.what_it_does: This is an "awesome" link list rather than software. It is organized into sections (Principle, Scalability, Availability, Stability, Performance, Intelligence, Architecture, Interview, Organization, Talk, Book), and each entry is a titled article or talk with the company or author named after "at" or a dash. The Scalability section is the largest, grouping links by topic such as microservices, distributed caching, locking, tracing, scheduling, monitoring, security, messaging and Kafka, logging, search, storage, relational and NoSQL databases, and CI/CD. Availability covers resilience, failover, load balancing, rate limiting and autoscaling. Stability covers circuit breakers, timeouts and bulkheads, and Performance covers OS and database tuning, garbage collection, media optimization and languages. The Intelligence section covers big data platforms and distributed machine learning. The README also points to contribution guidelines for adding or removing links.
use_cases: learning how large companies scale their systems
preparing for a system design interview
finding real-world case studies on caching, sharding or Kafka
looking up how big-data and ML platforms are built
notable: Organized by problem area: scalability, availability, stability, performance, and intelligence
Links grouped by specific technology such as Kafka, Cassandra, Redis, Elasticsearch and Airflow
Each entry names the company that published the case study
Includes principle-level reading such as CAP theorem, consistent hashing and chaos engineering
Entries are grouped by the kind of problem they address, such as 'if your system goes down'
caveats: Links are not verified in this summary and some may be outdated or no longer available; the README asks readers to submit pull requests for dead links
Not software: it provides no code to install or run
The README is truncated, so the Organization, Interview, Talk and Book sections were not visible
keywords: learn to build reliable large systems
